claim: The hepatitis B virus (HBV) is one of the most widespread human pathogens known today, with worldwide over 250 million people being infected.
source: The hepatitis B virus (HBV) is one of the most widespread human pathogens, with worldwide over 250 million people being infected, and an annual death toll of about 1 million globally (WHO, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2017

claim: HBV has an annual death toll of about 1 million globally.
source: The hepatitis B virus (HBV) is one of the most widespread human pathogens, with worldwide over 250 million people being infected, and an annual death toll of about 1 million globally (WHO, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2017

claim: In about 90–95% of cases, acute hepatitis B is self-limiting.
source: Infection of liver cells with HBV leads to acute hepatitis B, which is self-limiting in about 90–95% of cases.
evidence: Draws from established medical knowledge about HBV infection outcomes

claim: About 5–10% of infected individuals develop chronic infection of hepatitis B.
source: In about 5–10% of infected individuals virus clearance fails and patients develop chronic infection of hepatitis B, which puts them at lifelong elevated risk for liver cirrhosis and liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma).
evidence: Draws from established medical knowledge about HBV infection outcomes

claim: Chronic hepatitis B infection puts patients at lifelong elevated risk for liver cirrhosis and liver cancer.
source: In about 5–10% of infected individuals virus clearance fails and patients develop chronic infection of hepatitis B, which puts them at lifelong elevated risk for liver cirrhosis and liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma).
evidence: Draws from established medical knowledge about HBV complications

claim: HBV is usually transmitted by contact with infectious blood.
source: HBV is usually transmitted by contact with infectious blood, in highly endemic countries often during birth (WHO, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2017

claim: In highly endemic countries, HBV is often transmitted during birth.
source: HBV is usually transmitted by contact with infectious blood, in highly endemic countries often during birth (WHO, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2017

claim: HBV has a circular, partially double-stranded DNA genome of about 3.2kbp.
source: HBV has a circular, partially double-stranded DNA genome of about 3.2kbp that encodes four overlapping open reading frames (P, pre-S/S, pre-C/C, and X).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about HBV genome structure

claim: HBV genome encodes four overlapping open reading frames (P, pre-S/S, pre-C/C, and X).
source: HBV has a circular, partially double-stranded DNA genome of about 3.2kbp that encodes four overlapping open reading frames (P, pre-S/S, pre-C/C, and X).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about HBV genome structure

claim: HBVs are currently classified into eight genotypes (A-H) and numerous subgenotypes.
source: Based on the genomic sequence diversity, HBVs are currently classified into eight genotypes (A-H) and numerous subgenotypes that show distinct geographic distributions (Castelhano et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castelhano et al., 2017

claim: HBV genotypes show distinct geographic distributions.
source: Based on the genomic sequence diversity, HBVs are currently classified into eight genotypes (A-H) and numerous subgenotypes that show distinct geographic distributions (Castelhano et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castelhano et al., 2017

claim: All HBV genotypes are hypothesised to be primarily the result of recombination events.
source: All genotypes are hypothesised to be primarily the result of recombination events (Littlejohn et al., 2016; Simmonds and Midgley, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Littlejohn et al., 2016 and Simmonds and Midgley, 2005

claim: HBV evolution is driven to a lesser extent by the accumulation of point mutations.
source: To a lesser extent, HBV evolution is also driven by the accumulation of point mutations (Schaefer, 2007; Araujo, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schaefer, 2007 and Araujo, 2015

claim: The origin and evolutionary history of HBV are still unclear and controversial.
source: Despite being widespread and well-studied, the origin and evolutionary history of HBV are still unclear and controversial (Littlejohn et al., 2016; Souza et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Littlejohn et al., 2016 and Souza et al., 2014

claim: HBVs in non-human primates are phylogenetically closely related to, and yet distinct from, human HBV isolates.
source: HBVs in non-human primates (NHP), for instance in chimpanzees and gorillas, are phylogenetically closely related to, and yet distinct from, human HBV isolates, supporting the notion of an Africa origin of the virus (Souza et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Souza et al., 2014

claim: The phylogenetic relationship between NHP and human HBV supports the notion of an African origin of the virus.
source: HBVs in non-human primates (NHP), for instance in chimpanzees and gorillas, are phylogenetically closely related to, and yet distinct from, human HBV isolates, supporting the notion of an Africa origin of the virus (Souza et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Souza et al., 2014

claim: Molecular-clock-based analyses have resulted in conflicting estimates for the origin of HBV, with some as recent as about 400 years ago.
source: Molecular-clock-based analyses dating the origin of HBV have resulted in conflicting estimates with some as recent as about 400 years ago (Zhou and Holmes, 2007; Souza et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou and Holmes, 2007 and Souza et al., 2014

claim: Conflicting molecular clock estimates have raised doubts about the suitability of molecular dating approaches for reconstructing the evolution of HBV.
source: These observations have raised doubts about the suitability of molecular dating approaches for reconstructing the evolution of HBV (Bouckaert et al., 2013 , Souza et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouckaert et al., 2013 and Souza et al., 2014

claim: Ancient DNA research on HBV-infected mummies from the 16th century AD revealed a very close relationship between the ancient and modern HBV genomes.
source: Moreover, ancient DNA (aDNA) research on HBV-infected mummies from the 16th century AD revealed a very close relationship between the ancient and modern HBV genomes (Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012; Patterson Ross et al., 2018), indicating a surprising lack of temporal genetic changes in the virus during the last 500 years (Patterson Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012 and Patterson Ross et al., 2018

claim: There is a surprising lack of temporal genetic changes in HBV during the last 500 years.
source: Moreover, ancient DNA (aDNA) research on HBV-infected mummies from the 16th century AD revealed a very close relationship between the ancient and modern HBV genomes (Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012; Patterson Ross et al., 2018), indicating a surprising lack of temporal genetic changes in the virus during the last 500 years (Patterson Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patterson Ross et al., 2018

claim: Three ancient HBV genomes were recovered from human skeletons found at three different archaeological sites in Germany.
source: Here, we report the analysis of three ancient HBV genomes recovered from human skeletons found at three different archaeological sites in Germany.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Two Neolithic and one medieval HBV genome were reconstructed by de novo assembly from shotgun DNA sequencing data.
source: We reconstructed two Neolithic and one medieval HBV genome by de novo assembly from shotgun DNA sequencing data.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and methods described in the manuscript

claim: HBV-specific peptides were observed using paleo-proteomics.
source: Additionally, we observed HBV-specific peptides using paleo-proteomics.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LC-MS/MS analysis

claim: HBV has circulated in the European population for at least 7000 years.
source: Our results demonstrated that HBV has circulated in the European population for at least 7000 years.
evidence: Supported by radiocarbon dating and genomic data from Neolithic samples

claim: The Neolithic HBV genomes show a high genomic similarity to each other.
source: The Neolithic HBV genomes show a high genomic similarity to each other.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis of the ancient genomes

claim: The Neolithic HBV genomes do not group with any human-associated HBV genome in a phylogenetic network.
source: In a phylogenetic network, they do not group with any human-associated HBV genome and are most closely related to those infecting African non-human primates.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic network analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: The Neolithic HBV genomes are most closely related to HBV genomes infecting African non-human primates.
source: In a phylogenetic network, they do not group with any human-associated HBV genome and are most closely related to those infecting African non-human primates.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic network analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: The ancient viruses appear to represent distinct lineages that have no close relatives today and possibly went extinct.
source: The ancient viruses appear to represent distinct lineages that have no close relatives today and possibly went extinct.
evidence: Based on inference from phylogenetic analysis

claim: Evidence for presence of ancient HBV was detected in three human tooth samples.
source: We detected evidence for presence of ancient HBV in three human tooth samples as part of a metagenomic screening for viral pathogens that was performed on shotgun sequencing data from 53 skeletons using the metagenomic alignment software MALT (Vågene et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from metagenomic screening

claim: Metagenomic screening for viral pathogens was performed on shotgun sequencing data from 53 skeletons.
source: We detected evidence for presence of ancient HBV in three human tooth samples as part of a metagenomic screening for viral pathogens that was performed on shotgun sequencing data from 53 skeletons using the metagenomic alignment software MALT (Vågene et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental methods described

claim: The remains of the individuals were excavated from the Neolithic sites of Karsdorf (Linearbandkeramik [LBK], 5056–4959 cal BC) and Sorsum (Tiefstichkeramik group of the Funnel Beaker culture, 3335–3107 cal BC) as well as from the medieval cemetery of Petersberg/Kleiner Madron (1020–1116 cal AD), all located in Germany.
source: The remains of the individuals were excavated from the Neolithic sites of Karsdorf (Linearbandkeramik [LBK], 5056–4959 cal BC) and Sorsum (Tiefstichkeramik group of the Funnel Beaker culture, 3335–3107 cal BC) as well as from the medieval cemetery of Petersberg/Kleiner Madron (1020–1116 cal AD), all located in Germany (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by archaeological data and radiocarbon dating

claim: Deep-sequencing without any prior enrichment resulted in 367 to 419 million reads per sample.
source: After the three aDNA extracts had appeared HBV-positive in the initial virus screening, they were subjected to deep-sequencing without any prior enrichment resulting in 367 to 419 million reads per sample (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Table 1

claim: The Karsdorf sample yielded 3-fold genomic coverage of human DNA.
source: A principal component analysis (PCA) of the human DNA recovered from Karsdorf (3-fold genomic coverage) revealed that the sample clusters tightly with other contemporary early Neolithic individuals from the LBK (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by sequencing coverage data

claim: The Karsdorf sample clusters tightly with other contemporary early Neolithic individuals from the LBK in PCA analysis.
source: A principal component analysis (PCA) of the human DNA recovered from Karsdorf (3-fold genomic coverage) revealed that the sample clusters tightly with other contemporary early Neolithic individuals from the LBK (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The genetic makeup of the early LBK agriculturalists was distinct from the preceding western hunter-gatherers of Europe.
source: The genetic makeup of the early LBK agriculturalists was previously found quite distinct from the preceding western hunter-gatherers of Europe. The genetic shift between both populations was interpreted as a result of early farmers migrating from Western Anatolia into Central Europe introducing agriculture (Lazaridis et al., 2014; Haak et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lazaridis et al., 2014 and Haak et al., 2015

claim: The genetic shift between LBK agriculturalists and western hunter-gatherers was interpreted as a result of early farmers migrating from Western Anatolia into Central Europe introducing agriculture.
source: The genetic makeup of the early LBK agriculturalists was previously found quite distinct from the preceding western hunter-gatherers of Europe. The genetic shift between both populations was interpreted as a result of early farmers migrating from Western Anatolia into Central Europe introducing agriculture (Lazaridis et al., 2014; Haak et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lazaridis et al., 2014 and Haak et al., 2015

claim: The Sorsum sample yielded 1.2-fold genomic coverage of human DNA.
source: The almost 2000 years younger Sorsum individual (1.2-fold genomic coverage) clusters in the PCA most closely with individuals from the contemporary Funnel Beaker culture that inhabited Northern Germany at the end of the fourth millennium BCE (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by sequencing coverage data

claim: The Sorsum individual clusters in the PCA most closely with individuals from the contemporary Funnel Beaker culture.
source: The almost 2000 years younger Sorsum individual (1.2-fold genomic coverage) clusters in the PCA most closely with individuals from the contemporary Funnel Beaker culture that inhabited Northern Germany at the end of the fourth millennium BCE (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The Funnel Beaker culture population was quite admixed, as a result of a spatial and temporal overlap of early Neolithic farmers and remaining western hunter-gatherers for almost 2000 years.
source: This population was previously shown to be quite admixed, as a result of a spatial and temporal overlap of early Neolithic farmers and remaining western hunter-gatherers for almost 2000 years (Bollongino et al., 2013; Haak et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bollongino et al., 2013 and Haak et al., 2015

claim: The Petersberg sample yielded 2.9-fold genomic coverage of human DNA.
source: The Petersberg individual (2.9-fold genomic coverage), however, showed genetic affinities in the PCA with modern day central European populations.
evidence: Supported by sequencing coverage data

claim: The Petersberg individual showed genetic affinities in the PCA with modern day central European populations.
source: The Petersberg individual (2.9-fold genomic coverage), however, showed genetic affinities in the PCA with modern day central European populations.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis

claim: All three ancient human individuals are in agreement with the archeological evidence and radiocarbon dates for their respective time of origin.
source: All three ancient human individuals are therefore in agreement with the archeological evidence and radiocarbon dates for their respective time of origin.
evidence: Based on integration of genetic, archaeological, and radiocarbon data

claim: Typical aDNA damage patterns support the ancient origin of the obtained datasets.
source: Together with typical aDNA damage patterns (Figure 1—figure supplements 5–6), the human population genetic investigation supports the ancient origin of the obtained datasets.
evidence: Supported by aDNA damage pattern analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 5–6

claim: The Karsdorf HBV consensus sequence is 3183 nucleotides in length with 104-fold coverage.
source: The consensus genomes are 3161 (46-fold coverage), 3182 (47-fold coverage), and 3183 (104-fold coverage) nucleotides in length, which falls in the length range of modern HBV genomes and suggests that we successfully reconstructed the entire ancient HBV genomes (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by genome reconstruction data shown in Table 1

claim: The Sorsum HBV consensus sequence is 3182 nucleotides in length with 47-fold coverage.
source: The consensus genomes are 3161 (46-fold coverage), 3182 (47-fold coverage), and 3183 (104-fold coverage) nucleotides in length, which falls in the length range of modern HBV genomes and suggests that we successfully reconstructed the entire ancient HBV genomes (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by genome reconstruction data shown in Table 1

claim: The Petersberg HBV consensus sequence is 3161 nucleotides in length with 46-fold coverage.
source: The consensus genomes are 3161 (46-fold coverage), 3182 (47-fold coverage), and 3183 (104-fold coverage) nucleotides in length, which falls in the length range of modern HBV genomes and suggests that we successfully reconstructed the entire ancient HBV genomes (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by genome reconstruction data shown in Table 1

claim: The length of the ancient HBV consensus genomes falls in the length range of modern HBV genomes.
source: The consensus genomes are 3161 (46-fold coverage), 3182 (47-fold coverage), and 3183 (104-fold coverage) nucleotides in length, which falls in the length range of modern HBV genomes and suggests that we successfully reconstructed the entire ancient HBV genomes (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Based on comparison with known modern HBV genome lengths

claim: A peptide that is part of the HBV core protein was identified in the Karsdorf and Petersberg samples.
source: Further, when we conducted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) based bottom-up proteomics on tooth material from the three individuals, we identified in the Karsdorf and Petersberg samples a peptide that is part of the very stable HBV core protein, supporting the presence and active replication of HBV in the individuals' blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claim: The identification of HBV core protein peptide supports the presence and active replication of HBV in the individuals' blood.
source: Further, when we conducted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) based bottom-up proteomics on tooth material from the three individuals, we identified in the Karsdorf and Petersberg samples a peptide that is part of the very stable HBV core protein, supporting the presence and active replication of HBV in the individuals' blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Based on inference from proteomic data

claim: Phylogenetic network analysis was carried out with a dataset comprised of 493 modern HBV strains representing the full genetic diversity.
source: Phylogenetic network analysis was carried out with a dataset comprised of 493 modern HBV strains representing the full genetic diversity.
evidence: Supported by methods description

claim: The Neolithic HBV genomes branched off in two lineages in the phylogenetic analysis.
source: Strikingly, the Neolithic HBV genomes did not group with any human strain in the phylogeny. Instead, they branched off in two lineages and were most closely related to the African NHP genomes (Figure 2, 93% similarity).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic network analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: The Neolithic HBV genomes show 93% similarity to African NHP genomes.
source: Strikingly, the Neolithic HBV genomes did not group with any human strain in the phylogeny. Instead, they branched off in two lineages and were most closely related to the African NHP genomes (Figure 2, 93% similarity).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: The two Neolithic strains showed a higher genomic similarity to each other than to any other human or NHP genotype.
source: Although the two Neolithic strains were recovered from humans who had lived about 2000 years apart, they showed a higher genomic similarity to each other than to any other human or NHP genotype.
evidence: Supported by genomic comparison data

claim: The two Neolithic HBV genomes differed by 6% from each other.
source: Still, their genomes differed by 6% from each other and may therefore be considered representatives of two separate lineages.
evidence: Supported by genomic comparison data

claim: The two Neolithic HBV genomes may be considered representatives of two separate lineages.
source: Still, their genomes differed by 6% from each other and may therefore be considered representatives of two separate lineages.
evidence: Based on inference from genomic divergence data

claim: The Neolithic HBV genomes differed less than 8% from the African NHP strains.
source: They did, however, differ less than 8% from the African NHP strains and should therefore not be called a separate genotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by genomic comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The Neolithic HBV genomes should not be called a separate genotype.
source: They did, however, differ less than 8% from the African NHP strains and should therefore not be called a separate genotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on inference from genomic divergence data and genotype classification criteria

claim: The genome from the 1000-year-old Petersberg individual clustered with modern D4 genotypes.
source: The genome from the 1000-year-old Petersberg individual clustered with modern D4 genotypes.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis

claim: Some fragments of the Karsdorf sequences appeared to be very similar to modern human (G, E) and African NHP genotypes.
source: Some fragments of the Karsdorf sequences appeared to be very similar to modern human (G, E) and African NHP genotypes, and the Sorsum genome partially showed a high similarity to the human genotypes G, E and B. (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by recombination analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8

claim: The Sorsum genome partially showed a high similarity to the human genotypes G, E and B.
source: Some fragments of the Karsdorf sequences appeared to be very similar to modern human (G, E) and African NHP genotypes, and the Sorsum genome partially showed a high similarity to the human genotypes G, E and B. (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by recombination analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8

claim: It is conceivable that the older HBV from Karsdorf could have been a distant source for the younger Sorsum virus.
source: Given the close relationship between the two Neolithic virus genomes, it is also conceivable that the older HBV from Karsdorf could have been a distant source for the younger Sorsum virus (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on speculation from phylogenetic and recombination analysis

claim: The closer relationship between the Neolithic and the NHP strains compared to other human strains may have involved reciprocal cross-species transmission at one or possibly several times in the past.
source: The closer relationship between the Neolithic and the NHP strains compared to other human strains is noteworthy and may have involved reciprocal cross-species transmission at one or possibly several times in the past (Simmonds and Midgley, 2005; Souza et al., 2014; Rasche et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to Simmonds and Midgley, 2005; Souza et al., 2014; Rasche et al., 2016

claim: HBV already existed in Europeans 7000 years ago.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that HBV already existed in Europeans 7000 years ago and that its genomic structure closely resembled that of modern hepatitis B viruses.
evidence: Supported by radiocarbon dating and genomic data

claim: The genomic structure of ancient HBV closely resembled that of modern hepatitis B viruses.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that HBV already existed in Europeans 7000 years ago and that its genomic structure closely resembled that of modern hepatitis B viruses.
evidence: Supported by genomic comparison data

claim: Both Neolithic viruses fall between the present-day modern human and the known NHP diversity.
source: Both Neolithic viruses fall between the present-day modern human and the known NHP diversity.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis

claim: The two Neolithic HBV strains could be closely related to the remote ancestors of the present-day genotypes.
source: Therefore, it can be hypothesized that although the two Neolithic HBV strains are no longer observed today and thus may reflect two distinct clades that went extinct, they could still be closely related to the remote ancestors of the present-day genotypes, which is supported by signs of ancient recombination events.
evidence: Based on speculation supported by recombination analysis

claim: Signs of ancient recombination events support that the Neolithic HBV strains could be closely related to the remote ancestors of the present-day genotypes.
source: Therefore, it can be hypothesized that although the two Neolithic HBV strains are no longer observed today and thus may reflect two distinct clades that went extinct, they could still be closely related to the remote ancestors of the present-day genotypes, which is supported by signs of ancient recombination events.
evidence: Supported by recombination analysis data

claim: HBV evolution is characterized by recombination and point mutations and may be complicated by human-ape host barrier crossing.
source: As this evolution is characterized by recombination and point mutations and may further be complicated by human-ape host barrier crossing (Simmonds and Midgley, 2005; Souza et al., 2014; Rasche et al., 2016), genetic dating is not expected to yield meaningful results.
evidence: Supported by citations to Simmonds and Midgley, 2005; Souza et al., 2014; Rasche et al., 2016

claim: Genetic dating of HBV is not expected to yield meaningful results.
source: As this evolution is characterized by recombination and point mutations and may further be complicated by human-ape host barrier crossing (Simmonds and Midgley, 2005; Souza et al., 2014; Rasche et al., 2016), genetic dating is not expected to yield meaningful results.
evidence: Based on inference from the complex evolutionary characteristics of HBV

claim: TempEst analysis shows very little temporal signal in the HBV dataset.
source: This is additionally supported by a TempEst analysis (Rambaut et al., 2016) that shows very little temporal signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Supported by TempEst analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9

claim: The oldest genome (Karsdorf) was found in an individual that belonged to a population of early farmers that had migrated in the previous few hundred years from the Near East into central Europe.
source: It should, however, be noted that the oldest genome (Karsdorf) was found in an individual that belonged to a population of early farmers that had migrated in the previous few hundred years from the Near East into central Europe.
evidence: Based on archaeological and genetic evidence

claim: The close proximity to recently domesticated animals, changes in subsistence strategy and the adopted sedentary lifestyle might have contributed to the spread of HBV within Neolithic human populations.
source: One might speculate that the close proximity to recently domesticated animals, changes in subsistence strategy as well as the adopted sedentary lifestyle might have contributed to the spread of HBV within Neolithic human populations.
evidence: Based on speculation about factors affecting disease transmission

claim: HBV DNA can reliably be detected in tooth samples that are up to 7000 years old.
source: Based on our analysis, HBV DNA can reliably be detected in tooth samples that are up to 7000 years old.
evidence: Supported by successful detection and sequencing of HBV from ancient tooth samples

claim: Ancient HBV has so far only been identified in soft tissue from two 16th-century mummies.
source: Ancient HBV has so far only been identified in soft tissue from two 16th-century mummies (Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012; Patterson Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012 and Patterson Ross et al., 2018

claim: The aDNA analysis of HBV from prehistoric skeletons has not been described up to now.
source: The aDNA analysis of HBV from prehistoric skeletons, which facilitates evolutionary studies on a far-reaching temporal scale, has not been described up to now.
evidence: Based on review of prior literature

claim: HBV infection does not leave lesions on skeletal remains that would allow researchers to select affected individuals a priori.
source: One explanation for the difficulty of a molecular HBV diagnosis in bones is that the virus infection does not leave lesions on skeletal remains that would allow researchers to select affected individuals a priori, as it is the case for instance for leprosy (Schuenemann et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on knowledge of HBV pathology and comparison with other diseases

claim: The diagnosis of an HBV infection in skeletal populations is purely a chance finding.
source: The diagnosis of an HBV infection in skeletal populations is purely a chance finding and is thus more probable in a large-scale screening.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of skeletal lesions

claim: HBV biomolecules seem to be well preserved in teeth.
source: Overall, HBV biomolecules seem to be well preserved in teeth: Avoiding biases from DNA capture and reference-based mapping we could reconstruct three HBV genomes by de novo assembly from shotgun data and even observed HBV-specific peptides.
evidence: Supported by successful recovery of both DNA and peptides from ancient teeth

claim: The ratio of HBV genomes to the human genome was rather high and similar in all three samples (Karsdorf 35:1, Sorsum 40.2:1 and Petersberg 16:1).
source: The ratio of HBV genomes to the human genome in our samples was rather high and similar in all three samples (Karsdorf 35:1, Sorsum 40.2:1 and Petersberg 16:1).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Table 1

claim: There is no evidence that HBV DNA is more resistant to postmortem degradation than human DNA.
source: As there is no evidence that HBV DNA is more resistant to postmortem degradation than human DNA, the high rate of HBV compared to human DNA may reflect the disease state in the infected individuals at the time of death.
evidence: Based on knowledge of DNA degradation

claim: The high rate of HBV compared to human DNA may reflect the disease state in the infected individuals at the time of death.
source: As there is no evidence that HBV DNA is more resistant to postmortem degradation than human DNA, the high rate of HBV compared to human DNA may reflect the disease state in the infected individuals at the time of death.
evidence: Based on inference from the high HBV to human DNA ratio

claim: High copy numbers of viral DNA in the blood of infected individuals are associated with acute HBV infection, or reactivation of chronic HBV.
source: High copy numbers of viral DNA in the blood of infected individuals are associated with acute HBV infection, or reactivation of chronic HBV.
evidence: Based on established medical knowledge about HBV viral loads

claim: It seems likely that the death of the ancient individuals is related to the HBV infection, but might not be the direct cause of death.
source: Thus, it seems likely that the death of the ancient individuals is related to the HBV infection, but might not be the direct cause of death as fulminant liver failure is rather rare in modern day patients.
evidence: Based on inference from high viral loads and knowledge of HBV pathology

claim: Fulminant liver failure is rather rare in modern day HBV patients.
source: Thus, it seems likely that the death of the ancient individuals is related to the HBV infection, but might not be the direct cause of death as fulminant liver failure is rather rare in modern day patients.
evidence: Based on established medical knowledge about HBV outcomes

claim: The HBV infection might have contributed to other forms of lethal liver failure such as cirrhosis or liver cancer.
source: The HBV infection might have instead contributed to other forms of lethal liver failure such as cirrhosis or liver cancer.
evidence: Based on speculation about possible causes of death

claim: The Karsdorf individual is a male with an age at death of around 25–30 years, dated to 5056–4959 cal BC.
source: The investigated individual 537 is a male with an age at death of around 25–30 years (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), dated to 5056–4959 cal BC (KIA 40357–6116 ± 32 BP) (Brandt et al., 2014; Nicklisch, 2017).
evidence: Supported by archaeological and radiocarbon dating data

claim: The Sorsum individual is a male dated to 3335–3107 cal BC.
source: Individual XLVII 11 analyzed in this study is a male (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and dates to 3335–3107 cal BC (MAMS 33641–4501 ± 19 BP).
evidence: Supported by archaeological and radiocarbon dating data

claim: The Petersberg individual is a male with an age at death of around 65–70 years, dating to 1020–1116 cal AD.
source: The examined individual in grave 820 is a male with an age at death of around 65–70 years (Lösch, 2009 - Figure 1—figure supplement 3) dating to 1020–1116 cal AD (MAMS 33642–982 ± 17 BP).
evidence: Supported by archaeological and radiocarbon dating data

claim: The data set shows little positive correlation between genetic divergence and sampling time (correlation coefficient 0.075).
source: The data set shows little positive correlation between genetic divergence and sampling time (correlation coefficient 0.075) and there is very little temporal signal (TempEst R^2 = 0.006, see Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Supported by TempEst analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9

claim: There is very little temporal signal in the HBV dataset (TempEst R^2 = 0.006).
source: The data set shows little positive correlation between genetic divergence and sampling time (correlation coefficient 0.075) and there is very little temporal signal (TempEst R^2 = 0.006, see Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Supported by TempEst analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9
